title: Week 4 Weekly Reflection
text:
How did culture history bring order to the archaeological record, and which parts of its framework should archaeologists retain or reject today?
Urban and Schortman (2019) show how culture history organized archaeological materials through typology, chronology, and space-time systematics. They also show how concepts such as “culture,” “boundary,” and “periphery” shaped what archaeologists expected to find.
Feinman and Neitzel (2020) accept the need for chronology and spatial ordering but reject the assumptions built into culture-historical units: biological-cultural correspondence, homogeneity, discrete boundaries, primordial identity, and sudden collective change.
Choose one pathway and write a one-page, single-spaced reflection.

title: Week 2 Weekly Reflection
text:
How does archaeological “stuff” become evidence, and what limits the interpretations archaeologists can reasonably make from it?
Carver (2024) emphasizes that archaeological remains are shaped by complex formation processes involving deposition, decay, preservation, disturbance, and excavation. Their interpretation therefore depends on stratigraphic relationships and on reconstructing how deposits formed.
Wylie (2017) foregrounds the role of conceptual and technical scaffolding: the assumptions, methods, comparisons, and background knowledge that allow material traces to count as evidence. She argues that, when archaeologists rework that scaffolding, old data can sometimes “bite back” by calling established assumptions into question.
Write a one-page, single-spaced reflection addressing the focus question.

title: Week 3 — Levels of Archaeological Interpretation
text:
How can archaeologists move responsibly from material traces in the present to explanations of past human behavior, social organization, and historical change?
Archaeological evidence does not narrate the past by itself. Archaeologists observe artifacts, features, sediments, bones, chemical signatures, spatial distributions, buildings, and landscapes in the present. They then construct arguments that connect those observations to claims about activities, institutions, meanings, and processes that usually cannot be observed directly.
This makes Week 3 fundamentally about epistemology: how archaeological knowledge is possible, how it is justified, and how we decide whether one interpretation is better supported than another.
The central position developed in the lecture is:

Archaeological knowledge is theory-mediated but materially constrained.

“Theory-mediated” means that observations and interpretations depend on concepts, classifications, methods, comparisons, background knowledge, and research questions. “Materially constrained” means that archaeologists cannot simply make the past mean anything they want. Evidence can conflict with expectations, weaken an interpretation, support alternatives, and force researchers to revise what they thought they knew.

title: Week 3 — Levels of Archaeological Interpretation
text:
Exercise A: Identify the level
Classify each statement as low-level generalization, middle-level social explanation, high-level framework, or Binfordian linking argument.

Red-slipped pottery increases from Phase II to Phase III.
Greater settlement density increased opportunities for specialized exchange.
Experimental burning shows that this surface alteration forms above a particular temperature.
Historical materialism directs attention to relations between labor, surplus, and power.

Then explain why each belongs where you placed it.

title: Week 3 — Levels of Archaeological Interpretation
text:
Exercise B: Find the mechanism
Observation: larger settlements contain more craft workshops.
Generate two different mechanisms that could produce this relationship. For each, identify one additional archaeological expectation.

title: Week 3 — Levels of Archaeological Interpretation
text:
Exercise C: Testability
Choose an interpretation from an archaeological article and ask:

What observations support it?
What would make it less plausible?
Is there any possible observation the author would accept as contrary evidence?
Are alternatives compared?

title: Week 3 — Levels of Archaeological Interpretation
section: Exercise D: Strong versus weak theory
text:
Exercise D: Strong versus weak theory
Imagine that one artifact refuses to fit your typology.
A strong-theory response might classify it using the closest existing category.
A weak-theory response might pause and ask why the object resists the classification.
What new research question could the anomaly generate?

title: Week 3 — Levels of Archaeological Interpretation
text:
One-Sentence Summary
Archaeological interpretation becomes warranted not by removing theory, but by making explicit how material traces, linking arguments, testable social mechanisms, and broader theoretical frameworks work together—and by keeping every stage open to evidential challenge and revision.

title: Week 1 — Introduction
text:
Archaeologists study people who are no longer available to answer our questions. What survives is usually not a complete account of a past society but a damaged, selective, and transformed material record: artifacts, structures, soils, bones, plant remains, landscapes, images, inscriptions, and many other traces. These traces do not arrive with explanations attached.
That creates the central problem of Week 1:

How can archaeologists build reliable knowledge about human lives from material traces that do not speak for themselves?

The lecture begins with the silent archaeological record and the necessity of theory. It then asks why common sense is not enough, why archaeological observation is theory-laden, and how evidence can nevertheless resist our expectations. The second half carries the same problem into big data, machine learning, and generative AI. More data and more powerful algorithms do not remove interpretation; they introduce new layers of representation, selection, and potential bias.



Why can archaeological remains not simply “speak for themselves”?
What distinguishes observation, data, evidence, interpretation, and explanation?
Why is “common sense” not theory-free?
In what sense is archaeological observation theory-laden?
If observations are theory-laden, how can evidence still challenge expectations?
Why can several interpretations sometimes fit the same evidence?
How can multiple independent lines of evidence strengthen an inference?
Why does more data not automatically solve interpretation?
What is lost or transformed when material traces become digital data?
What should remain the responsibility of human archaeologists when AI is used?




By the end of Week 1, you should be able to explain why archaeological remains require interpretation; distinguish observation, data, evidence, interpretation, and explanation; identify assumptions connecting evidence to claims; explain theory-ladenness without concluding that “anything goes”; describe underdetermination and unproof; explain why multiple lines of evidence can strengthen inference; identify the proxy gap in computational archaeology; and critically evaluate AI-generated archaeological claims.

title: Week 1 — Introduction
text:
Fragmentation
The record is not incomplete merely because archaeologists have not excavated enough. Organic materials decay. Sites erode. objects are recycled. Landscapes change. Some activities leave little durable trace. Excavation and sampling are selective. We often cannot know exactly what has disappeared.

title: Week 1 — Introduction
text:
Underdetermination
Underdetermination occurs when the available evidence does not uniquely determine one interpretation.
Two explanations may both fit the surviving evidence. Additional evidence might distinguish them, but sometimes it may not.
This does not mean every imaginable explanation is equally good. Interpretations can still be criticized for contradicting evidence, requiring unsupported assumptions, ignoring contrary observations, depending on weak analogies, or violating chronology.

title: Week 1 — Introduction
text:
Unproof
Frieman uses unproof for gaps, ambiguities, unknowns, overlooked possibilities, and things that may remain unknowable.
Her argument is not that archaeologists should stop producing knowledge. It is that smoothing over uncertainty can create unwarranted certainty. Uncertainty can instead generate productive questions:

Which assumptions are doing the most work?
Whose lives have become archaeologically invisible?
Which alternatives have been excluded too quickly?
What evidence would distinguish between interpretations?
Which questions cannot currently be answered?


A responsible archaeological interpretation can be strong without pretending to be certain.

title: Week 1 — Introduction
text:
Inherited bias
A model can reproduce old assumptions because those assumptions are common in its training materials.

title: Week 1 — Introduction
text:
Hallucination
A generative model can produce fluent, plausible material that is unsupported or false. Fluency is not evidence.
For archaeology, this is especially dangerous because plausible stories can easily fill gaps in an already fragmentary record.

Plausibility is not the same as evidential support.

title: Week 1 — Introduction
text:
Critical deconstruction
Treat an AI response as an object for analysis:

What is its main claim?
What evidence does it provide?
Are the cited sources real and relevant?
What assumptions connect the evidence to the claim?
What alternatives are omitted?
Does the answer express uncertainty appropriately?
Can the claims be verified in original scholarly sources?

AI is not itself historical or archaeological evidence. Its output must be checked against the scholarly and material sources relevant to the question.

title: Week 1 — Introduction
section: Exercise A: From observation to explanation
text:
Exercise A: From observation to explanation
You excavate a grave containing an adult skeleton, a bronze object, two ceramic vessels, and animal bone.
Separate the following:

What could be directly observed?
What would need to be recorded as data?
What research questions could turn those data into evidence?
What interpretations might be proposed?
What assumptions would connect grave goods to social identity?
What alternative explanations should be considered?
What additional evidence would help discriminate among them?

The point is not to find one correct answer. The point is to expose the inferential steps.

title: Week 1 — Introduction
section: Exercise B: The record bites back
text:
Exercise B: The record bites back
Choose an archaeological claim from one of the readings. Ask:

What observations support it?
What result would make the claim less plausible?
Could the claim survive any possible evidence?

If no imaginable evidence could count against a claim, consider how archaeologists could evaluate it.

One-Sentence Summary
Archaeological interpretation is the disciplined, theoretically informed process of turning incomplete material traces into evidence-based claims while allowing the material record, alternative explanations, and acknowledged uncertainty to constrain what we can responsibly say about the past.

title: ARCL305: Archaeological Interpretation
text:
Land Acknowledgement
Throughout this course, we will gather at UBC Vancouver’s Point Grey Campus, located on the traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the xʷməθkʷəy̓əm (Musqueam) people. This land has been a place of learning for the Musqueam for millennia.

title: ARCL305: Archaeological Interpretation
text:
Course Description
This course introduces students to archaeological interpretation, with a focus on how archaeologists construct, evaluate, and revise explanations of the human past. We begin by examining the nature of archaeological evidence, the role of theory, archaeological classification, theoretical pluralism, and the logic of explanation and argument. We then explore how these interpretive approaches are applied to archaeological problems involving material culture and materiality, technology and skilled practice, mobility and migration, social networks, food and feasting, urbanism, Indigenous and collaborative archaeologies, and cognition and mind. Throughout the course, emphasis is placed on the relationship between theory and archaeological evidence: how concepts shape the questions archaeologists ask, how different forms of evidence support or constrain interpretation, and how competing explanations can be evaluated.

title: ARCL305: Archaeological Interpretation
text:
Course Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Explain key concepts, assumptions, and debates that shape archaeological

interpretation.

Distinguish among archaeological observations, data, evidence, inference,

interpretation, and explanation.

Evaluate archaeological arguments by examining their theoretical assumptions,

evidence, reasoning, and alternative explanations.

Apply theoretical concepts and analytical approaches to archaeological case

studies and datasets.

Compare different theoretical approaches and assess how they produce different

interpretations of the same or similar archaeological evidence.

Construct clear, evidence-based archaeological arguments and communicate

them effectively in discussion and writing.

title: ARCL305: Archaeological Interpretation
text:
Prerequisite
ARCL 203 (Archaeological Methods) or ARCL 103 (Introduction to Archaeology: Past Perspectives and Future Promise), or equivalent preparation in archaeology. Students who are uncertain about their preparation are encouraged to consult the instructor.

title: ARCL305: Archaeological Interpretation
text:
Required and Optional Readings
All required readings will be made available on Canvas. No specific textbook is required. Two readings are normally required for each instructional week. Additional readings listed in the schedule are optional and are provided for students who wish to explore a topic further, prepare for discussion, or develop a research essay.

title: ARCL305: Archaeological Interpretation
text:
Course Format
Class time will be divided approximately equally between lectures and group discussion sessions. Lectures will typically be held on Wednesdays to provide background and context for major themes, while group discussions will take place most Mondays. The schedule varies during weeks affected by holidays or the midterm break. For discussion sessions, the class will be randomly divided each week into small groups of five to six students. Students must complete the required readings in advance and be prepared to contribute substantive comments and critiques. Discussion contributions should engage directly with assigned readings and address specific arguments, evidence, concepts, or questions. Across the course, discussions will repeatedly return to four questions:

What is the author’s main claim?
What evidence supports it?
What theoretical assumptions connect the evidence to the interpretation?
What alternative interpretation might also account for the evidence?

Attendance and participation together account for 24% of the final grade:

Attendance and preparation: 8%
Discussion participation: 16%

This component evaluates regular attendance, preparation for discussion, substantive engagement with the readings, constructive participation in small-group discussion, and respectful engagement with other students’ interpretations. Students who miss more than one-third of class meetings without an approved academic concession or accommodation will receive no credit for the attendance and participation component.

title: ARCL305: Archaeological Interpretation
text:
Assignments

Weekly Reflections — 24%
Weekly reflections are designed to prepare students for discussion and to develop the habit of evaluating interpretations rather than accepting them at face value. Twelve reflections are assigned during the term: one for each topic in Weeks 2–9 and Weeks 11–14. Each reflection is worth 2% of the final grade. Students may complete each reflection through one of two equivalent pathways.

Pathway A: GenAI Critical Evaluation
Complete the required readings before consulting a generative AI system. The purpose of using AI is not to replace reading or generate a summary, but to help you question, test, and deepen your own interpretation of the scholarship. Follow this sequence: Read → Question → Consult AI → Verify → Reflect → Discuss Develop a focused question or interpretive problem from the readings, use a GenAI tool to explore it, and then compare the response carefully with the original texts. Your one-page, single-spaced reflection should focus primarily on your own analysis: what the AI response clarified, overlooked, distorted, or caused you to reconsider. At the end of the reflection, include the principal prompt or question you used and a brief statement explaining how GenAI contributed to your thinking. Full chat transcripts are not normally required.


Pathway B: Scholarly Critical Comparison
Students who prefer not to use a commercial GenAI system may complete an equivalent critical-comparison exercise. Instead of consulting an AI tool, compare two relevant scholarly interpretations or explanations drawn from the assigned, optional, or other appropriate scholarly readings, evaluate them against the assigned readings and archaeological evidence, and use that comparison as the basis for your reflection. Follow this sequence: Read → Question → Compare → Verify → Reflect → Discuss The reflection should identify the interpretive problem, explain where the two interpretations agree or differ, evaluate the evidence and assumptions supporting each, and state your own conclusion.



Submission and Evaluation
Reflections must be submitted online by the following Monday and will serve as the foundation for group discussion. Unless otherwise directed, in-class discussions are AI-free so that students can practice explaining, defending, and revising interpretations through direct engagement with one another. Reflections will be evaluated on engagement with the assigned readings, quality of the interpretive question, critical evaluation of the interpretation being examined, verification against original sources and archaeological evidence, and clarity of the student’s own analysis.


Research Essay — 28%
Students will complete a theory-driven research essay. The process involves:

selecting a subject, theory, or case study covered in the course;
developing a focused archaeological research question;
conducting library research and reviewing scholarly sources beyond the

assigned readings; and

writing an essay that examines how theoretical perspectives, models, and

concepts are used to interpret archaeological data, address research questions, and evaluate arguments. A proposed topic and preliminary research question must be submitted to the instructor for approval by 21 October 2026. A research essay outline, including a preliminary reference list of at least five scholarly sources (books, journal articles, or book chapters), normally including scholarship beyond the assigned course readings, is due 1 November 2026. The final essay will normally draw on a substantially larger body of relevant scholarship. No essay will be accepted unless the topic has been approved in advance. The final essay should be 10–12 double-spaced pages in 12-point font, excluding the title page and bibliography, and must follow the citation style of American Antiquity. Essays will be graded on the relevance and accuracy of theoretical engagement, interpretation of archaeological evidence, quality of argument and reasoning, clarity and organization, and proper referencing. The final essay is due 6 December 2026.


Generative AI and the Research Essay
Generative AI may be used as a support tool for activities such as brainstorming topics, refining research questions, exploring counterarguments, clarifying concepts, identifying organizational problems, or receiving feedback on writing you have already produced. GenAI may not substitute for library research, close reading, source evaluation, archaeological reasoning, or authorship. Do not rely on AI-generated summaries instead of reading sources, submit substantial AI-generated text as your own, or use AI-generated claims or references without independently verifying them. The argument, interpretation of evidence, and substantive analysis must be your own. If GenAI materially contributed to your work, include a brief AI Use Statement at the end of the essay identifying the tool and explaining how you used it and how you evaluated or revised its suggestions. Generative AI is not a scholarly source and should not be cited as evidence for an archaeological claim.


Final Examination — 24%
A take-home final examination will be distributed on 7 December 2026 and must be submitted no later than 13 December 2026. The examination will consist of six to eight essay questions. The examination instructions will specify how many questions must be answered and any length expectations. Students may use generative AI as a study tool before the examination is released. Once the examination has been released, however, generative AI may not be used to generate, develop, organize, rewrite, edit, or otherwise assist with examination answers unless the examination instructions explicitly state otherwise. The examination is intended to assess your own understanding of archaeological theory and your ability to synthesize course material and construct arguments independently.

title: ARCL305: Archaeological Interpretation
section: Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
text:
Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), including large language models and other systems that generate text, images, audio, or other content, is now part of the intellectual environment in which archaeological research and learning take place. This course therefore aims to teach students not simply whether AI can be used, but when it contributes to learning and when it interferes with it. The guiding principle for this course is augmentation rather than automation. GenAI can be useful when it helps you ask better questions, explore alternative interpretations, test an argument, clarify a concept, or identify weaknesses in your reasoning. It becomes counterproductive when it performs the intellectual work that you are expected to learn to do yourself. Permitted use varies by assessment and is stated in the relevant assignment instructions:

Weekly reflections: GenAI may be used through the structured critical-evaluation pathway; an equivalent non-GenAI scholarly critical-comparison

pathway is also available.

Research essay: GenAI may be used as a support tool within the limits stated

above.

Final examination: GenAI may not be used after the examination is released

unless the examination instructions explicitly permit a specific use.

In-class discussions and designated activities: normally AI-free unless otherwise

specified. Students remain responsible for the accuracy, integrity, and authorship of everything they submit.

title: ARCL305: Archaeological Interpretation
text:
Accuracy, Responsibility, and Disclosure
Generative AI can produce convincing but inaccurate information, invented references, distorted summaries, and biased or oversimplified interpretations. Important claims must therefore be checked against original scholarly sources. GenAI output should not be treated as archaeological evidence or scholarly authority. If AI-generated output itself is quoted, reproduced, or analyzed as an object of study, its source should be clearly identified in accordance with UBC guidance. Otherwise, permitted GenAI use should be disclosed/acknowledged through the required AI Use Statement rather than treated as scholarly citation. title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Week 1 established that archaeological remains do not interpret themselves. Week 2 asks a more concrete question:

What exactly is archaeological evidence, how did it become what survives today, and how do archaeologists turn physical remains into evidence about past human life?

The lecture begins with Martin Carver’s deliberately plain term “the stuff”: broken pottery, stone tools, animal bones, seeds, walls, pits, soils, collapsed buildings, refuse, and countless other physical traces. Archaeology starts with these material remains, but the remains encountered today are not intact copies of past life. They are the products of human action, abandonment, decay, burial, disturbance, preservation, excavation, classification, and interpretation.
past life ≠ archaeological record
The archaeological record is what survives after a long history of transformations.
Week 2 therefore moves through three connected problems:

What survives? — kinds and scales of archaeological evidence.
How did it survive? — context, formation processes, taphonomy, preservation, stratigraphy, and time averaging.
How does it become evidence? — conceptual scaffolding that makes physical traces relevant to claims about the past.

The required readings approach these problems from complementary directions. Carver emphasizes physical “stuff” and its continuous itinerary of decay. Renfrew and Bahn provide the vocabulary of artifacts, ecofacts, features, context, association, and formation processes. Lucas asks what kind of entity the archaeological record is and stresses formation, temporality, assemblages, and archaeological practice. Taylor and May show that stratigraphic recording is itself part of knowledge production. Wylie explains why evidence is constructed through conceptual and technical scaffolding yet can still surprise us and “bite back.”

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Spatial scales
microscopic attribute → artifact/ecofact → feature → activity area → assemblage → component → site → region → landscape
A microscopic residue may reveal what a vessel contained. Its position beside a hearth may help define an activity area. Repeated activity areas may reveal household organization. Household patterns across a settlement may reveal neighborhood structure. Settlement distributions across a valley may illuminate regional organization.
Different questions require different scales.

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Temporal scales
A stone flake may have been struck in less than a second. A hearth may represent hours or days. A house may accumulate deposits over decades. A tell may contain thousands of years.
Lucas emphasizes time averaging: materials deposited at different moments can become combined into one archaeological unit or assemblage. Archaeologists must ask whether a pattern represents one event, repeated behavior, or long-term accumulation.

Scale is not just size. Scale determines what kind of historical claim the evidence can support.

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Attributes
Attributes are observable or measurable properties: shape, dimensions, color, raw material, decoration, manufacturing traces, wear, chemistry, and residues.
Attributes matter because of research questions. Measurement alone does not create archaeological significance.

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Artifacts
Artifacts are portable objects made, modified, or used by humans. They may provide evidence about technology, craft, exchange, consumption, and identity, but must be interpreted through attributes, biographies, and contexts.

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Ecofacts
Ecofacts are biological or environmental remains of archaeological significance: animal bones, shells, seeds, charcoal, pollen, phytoliths, soils, and sediments.
They may reveal diet, agriculture, animal management, climate, vegetation, fuel use, and environmental modification.

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Features
Features are non-portable archaeological traces or modifications: hearths, postholes, pits, ditches, walls, floors, kilns, and graves.
A feature may contain several contexts—for example, a pit cut plus multiple fills and later disturbances.

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Exercise A: Context audit
Choose an artifact from the lecture. Record what can be learned from the object alone, what requires matrix, what requires provenience, what requires association, and what becomes unknowable if it was looted.

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Exercise B: Formation biography
Take an ordinary object and trace:
manufacture → use → maintenance → reuse → discard/loss → burial → natural transformation → later disturbance → excavation
Which stages leave traces? Which disappear?

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Exercise C: Pompeii premise
You find a room containing five pots, a grinding stone, animal bones, and ash. Produce one interpretation assuming a frozen activity moment and another assuming gradual accumulation, cleaning, reuse, and abandonment. What evidence would distinguish them?

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Exercise D: Harris matrix
Imagine natural soil; a pit cut into it; pit fill; a floor over the filled pit; a later posthole cutting the floor; and posthole fill. Put the units into relative order. Which relationships are observations, and which later groupings are interpretations?

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
section: Alison Wylie, “How Archaeological Evidence Bites Back”
text:
Alison Wylie, “How Archaeological Evidence Bites Back”
Focus on data and evidence as constructed rather than simply given; background knowledge and conceptual scaffolding; established categories and conventions; empirical resistance; and the possibility of putting old evidence to new uses.
Question: How can evidence be constructed through archaeological practice and still constrain archaeological claims?

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
Martin Carver, Chapter 1, “The Stuff”
Focus on material survival, decay, dispersal, preservation, “why do we have what we have?”, systemic and archaeological context, formation processes, ethnoarchaeology, experiment, and microscopic approaches.
Question: What processes transformed living places into the traces archaeologists encounter?

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
section: Gavin Lucas, Understanding the Archaeological Record
text:
Gavin Lucas, Understanding the Archaeological Record
Focus on competing meanings of “archaeological record”; remains versus archaeologist-produced archive; formation theory; systemic and archaeological context; time averaging; assemblages; and archaeological intervention.
Question: Is the archaeological record something surviving from the past, something archaeologists construct, or both?

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
section: Renfrew and Bahn, Chapter 2, “What Is Left?”
text:
Renfrew and Bahn, Chapter 2, “What Is Left?”
Focus on artifacts, ecofacts, features, sites, and regions; matrix, provenience, and association; primary/secondary context; cultural/natural formation; artifact life cycles; preservation; experiments; and superposition.
Question: Why must archaeologists reconstruct the history of a find before using it as evidence for behavior?

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
section: Taylor and May, “Resurrecting, Reinterpreting and Reusing Stratigraphy”
text:
Taylor and May, “Resurrecting, Reinterpreting and Reusing Stratigraphy”
Focus on stratigraphic units and Harris matrices; recording versus interpretation; grouping and phasing; digital archives; FAIR data; and reuse.
Question: What must be preserved so future researchers can reconstruct and challenge today’s interpretations?

title: Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
text:
One-Sentence Summary
Archaeological evidence is not simply what survives from the past but what archaeologists can responsibly infer from material traces after reconstructing their context, formation, temporal relationships, preservation histories, and the conceptual scaffolding through which those traces become relevant to claims about human history.

title: Week 4 — Culture History
text:
How did archaeologists make prehistory legible, and what happened when useful archaeological classifications came to be treated as real, bounded human groups?
Culture history solved one of archaeology’s first great problems. Archaeologists confronted enormous collections of artifacts, sites, architectural forms, burials, and styles that did not arrive with historical labels attached. Before archaeologists could explain why societies changed, they first had to establish what happened, to whom, when, and where.
Culture history supplied a powerful answer. It classified artifacts into recurring types, arranged them chronologically, mapped their geographic distributions, and combined those patterns into named archaeological cultures and regional sequences.
Its achievement was foundational:
MATERIAL REMAINS → TRAITS → TYPES → ASSEMBLAGES / COMPONENTS
        → PHASES → ARCHAEOLOGICAL CULTURES → HISTORICAL NARRATIVE
But the same system encouraged a major inferential shortcut:
recurring artifact pattern → shared cultural norms → bounded group → "a people"
The Week 4 lecture therefore makes two arguments at once. Culture history was a major methodological achievement, and archaeology still depends on classification, chronology, stratigraphy, typology, seriation, and spatial comparison. But the categories created by those methods should not automatically be treated as homogeneous peoples, ethnic groups, biological populations, or fixed historical actors.
The central lesson is:

Keep the chronology. Question the culture.

The Week 4 lecture therefore makes two arguments at once. Culture history was a major methodological achievement, and archaeology still depends on classification, chronology, stratigraphy, typology, seriation, and spatial comparison. But the categories created by those methods should not automatically be treated as homogeneous peoples, ethnic groups, biological populations, or fixed historical actors.
The central lesson is:

Keep the chronology. Question the culture.

title: Week 4 — Culture History
text:
Exercise A: Observation or interpretation?
For each statement, identify whether it is primarily an observation or interpretation.

Painted pottery increases from 12% to 48% between two dated intervals.
A new ethnic group entered the valley.
House form A occurs mostly east of the river.
The river marked a cultural boundary.
Genetic ancestry changes substantially after 2500 BCE.

Then identify what additional evidence would be needed for the interpretive claims.

title: Assignments
text:
This section provides assignment information and supporting materials for ARCL305: Archaeological Interpretation.
Official deadlines and submissions are managed through Canvas.

title: Assignments
text:
Weekly Reflections — 24%
Twelve weekly reflections are assigned during the term: Weeks 2–9 and 11–14. Each reflection is worth 2% of the final grade.
The reflections are designed to prepare for discussion and to develop the habit of evaluating archaeological interpretations rather than accepting them at face value.
Students may complete each reflection through one of two equivalent pathways:
Pathway A — GenAI Critical Evaluation
Read → Question → Consult AI → Verify → Reflect → Discuss
Pathway B — Scholarly Critical Comparison
Read → Question → Compare → Verify → Reflect → Discuss

Available Weekly Reflections

Week 2 — Archaeological Evidence
Week 3 — The Levels of Archaeological Interpretation
Week 4 — Culture History

Additional Weekly Reflections will be added as they are released.
Weekly reflection prompts and instructions will be added here as they are released.

title: Assignments
text:
Research Essay — 28%
Students will complete a theory-driven research essay examining how theoretical perspectives, models, and concepts are used to interpret archaeological data, address research questions, and evaluate arguments.
See the course syllabus for requirements, deadlines, and the course policy on permitted use of generative AI.

title: Assignments
text:
Final Examination — 24%
The course concludes with a take-home final examination.
See the course syllabus for examination dates, requirements, and the applicable generative-AI policy.

title: Week 3 Weekly Reflection
text:
How do different levels of archaeological theory work, and should middle-range theory be treated as a subtype of middle-level theory or as a distinct inferential task?
Urban and Schortman (2019) and Trigger (2006) both distinguish low-, middle-, and high-level theory and discuss middle-range theory as linking material observations to past behavior. Both relate middle-range theory to middle-level theory, but not in exactly the same way.
The lecture separates these tasks more sharply for analytical clarity, treating middle-level empirical theory as explanation of social mechanisms and Binfordian middle-range theory as linking traces to behavior and formation processes. Smith (2017) provides a further basis for evaluation through his emphasis on causal mechanisms and refutability.
Choose one pathway and write a one-page, single-spaced reflection.

title: Week 3 Weekly Reflection
text:
Pathway A — GenAI Critical Evaluation
Ask GenAI to explain the levels of theory and the relation between middle-level and middle-range theory.
Evaluate where it clarifies, conflates, or oversimplifies these concepts.

title: Week 3 Weekly Reflection
text:
Pathway B — Scholarly Critical Comparison
Compare Urban and Schortman (2019) with Trigger (2006) on the relation between middle-level and middle-range theory.
Use the lecture and Smith (2017) to assess which distinctions are most useful for constructing testable archaeological explanations.

title: Readings
text:
Required and optional readings are organized by week in the course syllabus.
Two readings are normally required for each instructional week. Additional readings are provided for students who wish to explore a topic further, prepare for discussion, or develop a research essay.

title: Readings
text:
Access to readings
Required reading files are provided through Canvas.
This public course website does not reproduce copyrighted books, chapters, or journal articles unless distribution is otherwise permitted.

title: Readings
text:
Using the readings
Students should complete the required readings before discussion sessions.
Across the course, reading and discussion repeatedly return to four questions:

What is the author’s main claim?
What evidence supports it?
What theoretical assumptions connect the evidence to the interpretation?
What alternative interpretation might also account for the evidence?

The weekly Study Guides provide additional guidance for working with the readings.
